title: Sugriva and Vali
hook: the monkey brothers; the arrow through the trees

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari, the forest woman who waited years and fed Rama the best berries. Your line was the sweet ones. Did you give the better piece away? Day fifty-five.

Two brothers. The older one, Vali, is king of the monkeys, enormously strong. One night a demon challenges him and runs into a cave, and Vali chases him in, telling his younger brother Sugriva to wait at the entrance. Sugriva waits. Days. Weeks. A whole year. Then blood comes pouring out of the cave, and he hears roaring, and he's sure his brother is dead. So he rolls a boulder over the entrance, goes home, and, at the kingdom's urging, becomes king. And then Vali walks out of the cave. Alive. He's won. And the first thing he sees is a rock sealing him in and his little brother on his throne. Today: a family fight, and the most argued-over arrow in the Ramayana.
screen: `VALI CHASES A DEMON INTO A CAVE.` → `SUGRIVA SEALS IT, THINKING HIM DEAD.` → `VALI WALKS OUT ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Vali doesn't believe it was a mistake. He drives Sugriva out, and, in Valmiki's telling, takes Sugriva's wife as well. Sugriva hides on a mountain with a few loyal friends, Hanuman among them. That's where Rama and Lakshmana find him. Two exiles, each missing a wife, each wronged. They make a pact over a fire: Rama will help Sugriva win back his kingdom, and Sugriva's monkey army will help find Sita. Sugriva wants proof Rama can beat his brother, so Rama sends one arrow through a row of seven great sala trees. Then the plan. Sugriva goes to Vali's gate and roars a challenge. Rama waits behind the trees. But the brothers fight, and Rama can't tell them apart, so he doesn't shoot, and Sugriva is beaten badly. The second time, Sugriva wears a garland of flowers so Rama knows him. And this time, from behind the trees, Rama shoots Vali. Vali falls, and he's furious, and he has a point. You shot me from hiding, he says. I wasn't even fighting you. Rama answers: you took your brother's wife while he lived, and a king, and his allies, must punish that. Vali, dying, accepts it, and asks Rama to look after his son Angada. Remember that name. People have argued about this arrow for over two thousand years. Some say Rama upheld dharma, the right order of things, and kept his promise to an ally. Others say it's the one act in his story that doesn't sit right. The Ramayana itself lets Vali make his case out loud. It doesn't cut him off. That's the lesson under the lesson: when you pick a side in someone else's family fight, you inherit the whole fight.
screen: `TWO EXILES MAKE A PACT.` · `ONE ARROW THROUGH SEVEN TREES.` · `THE SHOT FROM BEHIND THE TREES.` · `VALI MAKES HIS CASE, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breathing settle. Bring to mind a fight between two people you love. Brothers, sisters, parents, two friends. Don't pick a side yet. Hear the first one's story in your head, as fairly as you can. Now hear the second one's story, just as fairly. Notice where each of them has a point. Notice where each of them is hurt. You don't have to fix anything today. Just hold both stories, side by side, for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Sugriva and Vali. Two monkey brothers split by a sealed cave, and an arrow people still argue about.
Your line: choose a side carefully. Today, before you agree with someone about a person who isn't in the room, ask what the other side would say. Day fifty-five.

howItsDone: The killing of Vali is one of the Ramayana episodes Hindu teachers and commentators debate most openly; in temple talks, in Ramlila, and in classical commentaries it is taught alongside Vali's objection and Rama's answer.

fork.setup: you're Rama, hidden behind the trees. the two brothers are fighting, and they look exactly alike. what do you do?
options: step out and stop the fight.
fork.reveal: he holds the arrow, and Sugriva is beaten badly. the second time, Sugriva wears a garland of flowers so Rama can tell them apart.

original.note: Sanskrit: su (good, beautiful) + griva (neck). Sugriva, the one with the handsome neck.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hero shoots a villain.
what it means: two brothers split by a mistake, and a shot from behind the trees that the story lets the dying Vali protest.
what a scholar hears: Vali's objection and Rama's reply are in the Kishkindha Kanda itself; commentators have debated the arrow for centuries.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (the pact; the seven sala trees; the two duels; Vali's death and his objection, roughly sargas 5–18)

notes: The cave story (Vali chasing the demon Mayavi; Sugriva sealing the cave after a year) is Sugriva's own account in Valmiki; confirm the 'a whole year' detail.
